A wave function n m r , ( ) , , for a one-electron atom in the state (n, ,, m) is called an ­orbital. This term recalls the circular orbits of the Bohr atom, but there is no real resemblance. An orbital is not a trajectory traced by an individual electron. When the one-electron atom is in state (n, ,, m), it is conventional to say the elec- tron is “in an (n, ,, m) orbital.” This phrase is merely a shorthand way of making the precise but cumbersome statement: “When an electron has energy, total angu- lar momentum, and z component of angular momentum values corresponding to the quantum numbers n, ,, m, the probability density of finding the electron at the point ( ) r, , is given by n m r , 2 ( ) , , . Do not allow this verbal shorthand to mis- lead you into thinking an orbital is some sort of “region in space” inside which the electron is confined.
